So the heart can regain its gradient to pump. The next one I'm seeing here is I think it's amyloidosis. Amyloidosis cancel, do the same thing.

You're right to see the functional similarity. In constrictive pericarditis, **the pericardium is a rigid scar** that prevents diastolic filling, causing **equalization of diastolic pressures across all four chambers**. The heart itself is normal — you just need to **remove the shell with pericardiectomy** to restore the gradient.

Now amyloidosis: **the infiltrate is inside the wall**, not outside. **Amyloid fibrils deposit in the myocardium itself**, making the ventricle stiff and noncompliant. The pericardium is normal. So pressures still rise and equalize, but **you cannot cut away the disease** — it's woven into the muscle. That's why **low voltage on EKG despite thick walls on echo** is your bedside clue: amyloid replaces conducting tissue, while the infiltrated myocardium looks bulky but generates weak electrical signal.
So what are some sources of amyloid or whatever that got deposited in the? What are some of the sources?

The misfolded protein is the source. In primary amyloidosis (AL), **plasma cells in the bone marrow produce excess immunoglobulin light chains** that misfold and deposit in the heart, kidneys, tongue, and nerves. In secondary amyloidosis (AA), **chronic inflammation** — tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease — drives the liver to churn out **serum amyloid A protein**, which deposits in kidneys and spleen, rarely the heart. Then there's **transthyretin amyloid (ATTR)**: either **wild-type** from aging liver or **mutant** from genetic variants — this one loves the heart and carpal tunnel. So at the bedside, **ask yourself: marrow, inflammation, or liver?** That guides your biopsy and treatment fork.
why isnit the answr constictive pericarditis

Because **the heart in this case is the source of the stiffness, not the victim of a scar**. In constrictive pericarditis, the pericardium is thickened and calcified — the myocardium is normal. You'd expect **septal bounce on echo**, **respiratory variation in mitral inflow**, and **a pericardial knock** on exam. Here, the infiltrated ventricle itself is rigid. **Low voltage on EKG with thick walls on echo** is pathognomonic for amyloid — you cannot explain that with a normal heart trapped in a scar. The constrictor's heart squeezes well but can't fill; the amyloid heart can't squeeze well and can't fill. **That electrical-mechanical dissociation rules out constriction.**

You're asking about the nose — that's a key spatial clue. **Amyloid deposits in the nasal mucosa and submucosa**, causing **fragile capillaries that bleed easily**. The liver isn't clearing the misfolded protein fast enough, so **light chains or transthyretin accumulate in tissues with high blood flow and fenestrated capillaries** — the nose, tongue, kidneys, and heart. **Epistaxis in this patient isn't from trauma or hypertension; it's from infiltrated, brittle vessels.** The same process that stiffens his heart also makes his nose bleed. One protein, two locations, same mechanism.
so basically changign th ecompositoion of th evesels and making them weak

Exactly. **Amyloid fibrils physically replace the normal structural proteins in the vessel wall**, like scaffolding made of glass instead of steel. The vessel becomes **rigid, brittle, and unable to vasoconstrict properly** when injured. So a minor sniff or dry air that would make a normal vessel pinch shut instead causes a **fissure that won't seal** — that's the epistaxis. Same reason he may have **easy bruising** and **periorbital purpura** (raccoon eyes) from a sneeze or bending over. **The vessel composition is the mechanism: infiltrated, not inflamed.**
